design_detail: PROSPERO-registered systematic review and three-level meta-analysis with robust variance estimation of studies published May 2017–May 2025 (designed not to overlap Potvin et al., 2018): 68 independent studies, 242 effect sizes, 5244 people with methamphetamine use disorder and 3801 healthy controls, in 13 domains including self-reported impulsivity. Abstinence modelled by phase and by restricted cubic splines; GRADE certainty by domain.
can_establish: The average difference between people with methamphetamine use disorder and healthy controls in the 2017–2025 literature, its spread across settings (prediction intervals), and whether study samples tested at different abstinence durations differ on average.
cannot_establish: That methamphetamine caused the differences, that cognition does or does not recover within people (all comparisons are between different studies' samples), or clinical significance for individuals (prediction interval includes zero).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (meta-analysis). Included studies' samples: 87.2% male; 36 'exclusive' use-disorder samples, 18 polysubstance, 14 with psychiatric comorbidity (p. 6).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Adults with DSM or ICD methamphetamine use disorder, including those with polysubstance use or psychiatric comorbidity; healthy controls without substance use disorders (nicotine and caffeine allowed); validated tests or self-report impulsivity; cross-sectional or baseline data; abstinence verified. Excluded: under 18; traumatic brain injury, stroke, epilepsy or HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder; testing within 48 hours of last use or without documented abstinence; non-English (p. 2).
sample.demographics: Education 9.94 vs 11.33 years; weighted mean duration of use 7.38 years; abstinence 4.2–971 days, weighted mean 248.2 days (p. 6).
sample.selection_effects: Only 10.3% of studies reported outcomes beyond 12 months of abstinence (p. 10); 51.5% of studies met the paper's quality threshold (p. 6).

exposure.measurement: As in the primary studies; abstinence verified by biological testing, clinical assessment or study protocol (p. 2).
exposure.polysubstance: Included by design to reflect treatment populations; compared as subgroups (p. 2).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 48 hours; phases defined as under 1 month (described as the acute withdrawal phase), 1–12 months and over 12 months (p. 5).

comparison.controls: Healthy controls without substance use disorders other than nicotine or caffeine and without current neurological or psychiatric conditions (p. 2).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No premorbid ability; age, sex and education available only as study averages (p. 10).

outcomes.instruments: Performance tests and self-report impulsivity scales coded into 13 domains using MATRICS, the unity/diversity model of executive function and RDoC (p. 4).
outcomes.operationalization: Hedges' g, negative = users worse; overall estimate pools all 13 domains including self-reported impulsivity (pp. 1, 6).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Benjamini–Hochberg for omnibus domain and subgroup tests; spline trend tests unadjusted and labelled exploratory (p. 4).

analysis.effect_sizes: Overall g=−0.68 (95% CI −0.77 to −0.58), Q(241)=1379.6, I²=85.3% (35.7% between studies, 49.6% within), 95% prediction interval −1.58 to 0.22 (p. 6). By domain (Table 2, p. 7): visuospatial −1.09 (7 studies), shifting −0.86, self-reported impulsivity −0.86 (27), planning −0.82, verbal learning and memory −0.79 (17), processing speed −0.74, attention −0.67, visual learning and memory −0.64, verbal fluency −0.53, inhibitory control −0.50 (19), decision-making −0.50, working memory −0.45, social cognition −0.42 (12); domains did not differ significantly (F(12,140.1)=2.07, P=0.10) (p. 6). Abstinence phases: under 1 month −0.70 (15 studies), 1–12 months −0.63 (35), over 12 months −0.88 (7); F(2,14.9)=1.20, P=0.33 (p. 7). Splines: no trend for inhibitory control (17 studies, 7–265 days) or self-reported impulsivity (21, 23–280 days) (p. 7). Sex: higher proportion of men associated with smaller differences, β=0.518 (0.079–0.957), P=0.03 in the fully adjusted model (p. 6). Comorbidity subgroups did not differ (P=0.26), equivalence indeterminate (pp. 6–7). Publication bias: overall Egger P=0.32, trim-and-fill −0.65; domain-level Egger P=0.005 (verbal learning and memory) and P<0.001 (working memory) (p. 7).
analysis.covariates: Age, sex and education (study level) in multivariable meta-regression (p. 4).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD420251004391 (p. 2); deviations not discussed in the main text.
analysis.selective_reporting: Domain-level publication-bias signals for verbal learning/memory and working memory are attributed to lower test reliability in smaller domains (p. 7), though these domains have 14–17 studies.
analysis.power: Abstinence and comorbidity comparisons acknowledged as underpowered (pp. 9–10).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Samples of people with methamphetamine use disorder scored on average two-thirds of a standard deviation below healthy controls, with very large heterogeneity and a prediction interval running from large deficits to none; samples tested at different abstinence durations did not differ significantly, with few studies beyond a year.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The conclusions describe the impairment as generalized and clinically significant and state that passive abstinence fails to restore cognitive function across short-, medium- and long-term windows (p. 10). Clinical significance is not shown by standardized group differences, the pooled 'neurocognitive' estimate includes questionnaire-measured impulsivity, and the abstinence result compares different samples rather than following people over time, as the paper itself says in the note to Figure 3 (p. 9); the long-term phase rests on 7 studies and the spline models on the first nine months (p. 10).

timeline.event: Earlier meta-analysis on the pre-2017 literature, which this review deliberately does not overlap

replication.where_it_stands: Published 2026; no commentary or replication yet. Its visuospatial finding contradicts the relative sparing reported by Potvin et al. (2018); its sex finding runs opposite to Scott et al. (2007).

funding.funder: National Science and Technology Major Projects for Science, Technology and Innovation 2030, China (2021ZD0202102) (p. 1).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no conflicts of interest (p. 1).
funding.affiliations_note: A large language model was used for language editing, according to the acknowledgments (p. 10). Extraction data available on request only (p. 1).

what_would_settle_it: Within-person longitudinal studies across 1–3 years of abstinence with retested controls and premorbid estimates; separating questionnaire impulsivity from performance measures in pooled estimates.

domains.note: Four databases, 2017–2025, English only, manual reference screening (p. 2).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Methodologically the most advanced of the four meta-analyses. Confidence in its conclusions is limited less by its methods than by its interpretation: pooling questionnaire impulsivity into a cognitive estimate, causal and clinical language for cross-sectional group differences, and an upgrade for large effect in GRADE despite a plausible confounder (education 9.9 vs 11.3 years). All domains ended at very low certainty in its own GRADE.

key_findings.finding: 68 studies (2017–2025), 5244 users and 3801 controls; overall g=−0.68 (95% CI −0.77 to −0.58) with a prediction interval of −1.58 to 0.22.
key_findings.locator: Results, Study Characteristics and Overall Cognitive Impairment; Abstract
key_findings.note: Page numbers are those of the online-first PDF.

key_findings.finding: The overall estimate pools 13 domains including self-reported impulsivity (g=−0.86, 27 studies), a questionnaire rather than a performance measure.
Domain estimates ranged from −0.42 (social cognition) to −1.09 (visuospatial, 7 studies); no significant differences between domains.
key_findings.note: The printed P=0.10 does not match the printed F(12, 140.1)=2.07, which gives p≈0.023 (editors' calculation; see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Samples tested under 1 month, 1–12 months and over 12 months abstinent did not differ (−0.70, −0.63, −0.88; P=0.33); only 7 studies over 12 months.
key_findings.note: Four of the 7 studies in the over-12-month stratum are large samples (326–567 users: Chen et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2022; Jiang et al., 2025; Tian et al., 2022; Table 1, pp. 3–4), so that estimate rests heavily on a few cohorts; the authors attribute its larger size to sample selection (p. 7).

key_findings.finding: GRADE certainty was very low for all 13 domains.
Studies with more men showed smaller differences (β=0.518, P=0.03), an ecological association the authors warn against reading at the individual level.
Users had 9.94 vs controls' 11.33 years of education; education did not significantly moderate effects at the study level.

Domain-level Egger tests were significant for verbal learning and memory (P=0.005) and working memory (P<0.001) and below the paper's own P<0.10 criterion for shifting (P=0.055) and self-reported impulsivity (P=0.066); overall Egger P=0.32, trim-and-fill adjusted g −0.65.
key_findings.locator: Sensitivity Analyses and Publication Bias; Table 2

reporting_issues.issue: The conclusion that passive abstinence fails to restore cognition (p. 10) contradicts the paper's own caution that its cross-sectional estimates should not be read as individual remission trajectories (Figure 3 note, p. 9).
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstinence finding means 'no detectable difference between samples', not 'no recovery'.

reporting_issues.issue: GRADE upgrading for large effect (|g|≥0.80) is applied to cross-sectional comparisons with an obvious candidate confounder (education).
reporting_issues.consequence: No effect on the final ratings (all very low), but the reasoning is not standard.

reporting_issues.issue: The between-domain omnibus test is printed as F(12, 140.1)=2.07, P=0.10, but the printed F and degrees of freedom give p≈0.023 (editors' calculation), whereas the comorbidity and abstinence-phase tests match their printed p-values; the paper applies Benjamini–Hochberg correction to the domain and comorbidity omnibus tests (p. 4) but does not say this value is adjusted.
reporting_issues.consequence: Even adjusted over those two tests the domain p would be about 0.045, so the statement that domains did not differ, and the reading of the impairment as generalized, may not hold.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 contains pairs of entries with near-identical sample characteristics that may be the same participants counted twice: Fitzpatrick et al. 2020 and 2021 (both 108 users and 50 controls, 81/38 men); Wang et al. 2024 and Zhou et al. 2024 (46/44 vs 45/43, the same mean ages 31.4/26 and education 11.5); Luo et al. 2024, S4 and S59 (102/51 vs 96/46, near-identical age, abstinence and years of use).
reporting_issues.consequence: If these overlap, the 68 independent studies overstate independence; this cannot be settled without the primary papers.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 marks planning and problem solving (Egger P=0.986) and inhibitory control (P=0.128) as downgraded for publication bias, although the footnote criterion is Egger P<0.10 and the text names four domains meeting it.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: every domain ends at very low certainty either way, but the downgrading is not applied as stated.

verification.source_read: PDF (online-first), pp. 1–11 (all pages; supplements not read)

disagreements.reviewer: Wrong location: content correct; Methods, Outcomes is on p. 2 (right column), not p. 4 (p. 4 has the domain-coding section); the pooling of all 242 effect sizes including self-reported impulsivity is shown in Figure 2 (p. 8); pages should read pp. 2, 7–8.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed on pp. 2, 4, 7 and 8. Data unchanged.

disagreements.reviewer: Confirmed; add: the printed omnibus P=0.10 does not match F(12, 140.1)=2.07, which gives p≈0.023 unless the value is FDR-adjusted (not stated).
disagreements.resolution: Recomputed (F distribution, 12 and 140.1 df): p=0.0226. Added as a note and as a reporting issue.

disagreements.reviewer: Missed: the over-12-month abstinence stratum (7 studies) includes four large samples of 326–567 users (Chen 2022, Jiang 2022, Jiang 2025, Tian 2022; Table 1), so the −0.88 estimate rests heavily on a few cohorts.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed in Table 1: the seven studies with mean abstinence over 365 days are Bensmann 2019 (24 users), Chen 2022 (326), Jiang 2022 (428), Jiang 2025 (559), Liu 2022 (45), Su 2023 (25) and Tian 2022 (567). Added as a note.

disagreements.first_pass: Domain-level publication-bias tests were significant for verbal learning and memory (P=0.005) and working memory (P<0.001); overall Egger P=0.32.
disagreements.reviewer: Confirmed; also shifting (P=0.055) and self-reported impulsivity (P=0.066) were below 0.10 (Table 2).
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed in Table 2 (p. 7); the paper's criterion for a publication-bias signal is Egger P<0.10 (Table 2 footnote; text p. 7). Finding completed.

disagreements.reviewer: Missed: the domain omnibus test F(12, 140.1)=2.07 corresponds to p≈0.023, not the printed P=0.10 (p. 6); the statement that domains did not differ may depend on an unstated adjustment.
disagreements.resolution: Recomputed: domain p=0.023; comorbidity F(2, 30.8)=1.42 gives 0.26 and abstinence F(2, 14.9)=1.20 gives 0.33, both as printed; Benjamini–Hochberg over the two stated tests gives 0.045 for domains. Added.

disagreements.reviewer: Missed: possible overlapping samples counted as independent studies (Table 1, pp. 3–4): Fitzpatrick 2020/2021; Wang 2024/Zhou 2024; Luo 2024 (S4/S59); cannot be verified without the primary papers.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed the printed values in Table 1. Added, worded as a possibility.
Found while checking key finding 7 on a 220-dpi render of Table 2 (p. 7): six domains carry the publication-bias mark, four meet the stated criterion. Added as a minor reporting issue.
